charts.title: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Komatsu Ltd.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Komatsu Ltd.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Komatsu Ltd.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Komatsu Ltd.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Komatsu Ltd.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Komatsu Ltd.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Komatsu Ltd.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Komatsu Ltd.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Komatsu Ltd.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue: CMU vs Retail Finance
segmentRevenue.content:
Komatsu reports two segments: Construction, Mining & Utility Equipment (CMU) -- the core heavy-equipment manufacturing business -- and Retail Finance, the captive arm that finances dealer and customer purchases of that equipment.

For Komatsu Ltd.: Retail Finance revenue is interest and fee income on a lease/loan book, not equipment sales, so it moves on different drivers (financing volume, rates) than CMU and should not be read as organic growth.

What to watch:

  • CMU revenue as the cyclical driver -- it tracks mining capex and construction activity
  • Retail Finance growing faster than CMU can signal looser financing terms supporting sales

segmentProfit.title: Segment profit: CMU vs Retail Finance
segmentProfit.content:
Segment profit (operating income) for the same two segments. Retail Finance typically runs a much higher margin on a much smaller revenue base, since it is a spread business rather than a manufacturer.

For Komatsu Ltd.: CMU profit is where the mining up-cycle or down-cycle actually shows up; a Retail Finance profit decline usually reflects credit losses or funding-cost pressure, not demand for equipment.

What to watch:

  • CMU margin trend versus the regional revenue mix below (higher-margin markets like North America and Oceania mining versus lower-margin markets)
  • Retail Finance credit quality if CMU sales slow (dealers/customers carrying more leverage)

cmuRegion.title: CMU segment revenue by region
cmuRegion.content:
The Construction, Mining & Utility segment's revenue split across ten regions: Japan, North America, Latin America, Europe, CIS, China, Asia (ex-China/Japan), Middle East, Oceania and Africa. Shown FY-only since the regional split is disclosed annually, not every interim period.

For Komatsu Ltd.: North America and Oceania are the mining-capex-driven regions that carry Komatsu's earnings cycle; China has been structurally weak for several years on a depressed construction market, while CIS revenue collapsed after Russia-related sanctions and exits. The regional mix is the clearest read on where the next up- or down-cycle is coming from, which a single consolidated Revenue line hides.

What to watch:

  • North America / Oceania share of CMU revenue -- the mining-cycle bellwether
  • China's continued softness versus any stabilisation
  • CIS revenue post-2022 as a structural step-down, not a cyclical dip

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Komatsu Ltd.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
